title: Disaster Recovery Testing
summary: Disaster recovery testing is the planned exercise of restoring systems and data from backups and alternative arrangements in order to prove that recovery targets can actually be met. A test is designed around measurable objectives, usually a recovery time objective for how long an outage may last and a recovery point objective for how much data may be lost, and it must produce evidence: how long the restore took, what failed, and which runbook step was wrong. Tests range from a tabletop walkthrough, through restoring selected systems into an isolated environment, up to a full failover carrying production traffic, and each level exposes different problems. The common mistake is testing only that a backup job reported success, which says nothing about whether the data can be read back and used. An untested restore is an assumption, and the first real test should never be the incident itself.

exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Disaster Recovery Testing - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

beginner.definition: Disaster recovery testing means practising the work of bringing systems back after a serious failure. The team restores data from backups and checks whether services work again. The aim is to prove that a plan on paper actually works in practice.
beginner.whyItMatters: A backup that has never been restored is only a hope. Many teams discover during a real outage that a backup was empty or too slow. Testing shows how long recovery really takes and what is missing. It also gives people practice, so they act calmly under pressure. Regulators and customers often ask for proof that the plan works.
howItWorks: The team agrees targets, such as how long an outage may last and how much data may be lost.
They write a plan that says who does what, and in which order.
On a chosen date they restore systems into a safe test area.
They time each step and write down every problem that they meet.
They compare the result with the agreed targets and decide what to fix.
They update the plan and repeat the test on a regular schedule.
beginner.example: Think of a fire drill in a large office building. The alarm sounds on an ordinary Tuesday, and everyone walks to the meeting point. The wardens time how long the building takes to empty. They notice that one back stairwell door was locked and that two new staff did not know the route. Nobody is in danger, but the building is now safer because of what the drill showed. If the first real fire were also the first practice, the mistakes would cost far more. Recovery testing is the fire drill for your systems.
takeaways: A backup you have never restored is not a proven backup.
Write down real times and real failures, then fix the plan.
Run drills on a schedule, and include the people who respond.

objectives: Explain what disaster recovery testing is and what it is meant to prove.
Explain recovery time objective and recovery point objective in plain terms.
Describe the different levels of test, from tabletop to full failover.
Identify the evidence a test should produce and how it drives plan changes.
Explain why a successful backup job is not proof of recoverability.
